A Practical Guide to B2B, B2C and D2C Business Models By Team TradersInd / November 5, 2026 What Is B2B? A Practical Guide to B2B, B2C and D2C Business Models Understand the differences between B2B, B2C and D2C business models. Businesses use different models to sell products and services. Some sell directly to individual customers. Others supply products to retailers, manufacturers, distributors and commercial buyers. Understanding these business models helps business owners choose the right customers, suppliers and sales channels. Three commonly used terms are B2B, B2C and D2C . Although they all describe commercial activities, they work in different ways. This guide explains what B2B means, how it differs from B2C and D2C, how businesses work with suppliers, and what buyers should consider before placing an order. What Is B2B? B2B stands for Business-to-Business . It describes commercial transactions between two businesses. In this model, one business supplies products or services to another business. The buyer may use those products in its operations, manufacture another product, resell them or deliver services to its own customers. For example: A manufacturer supplies industrial pumps to a factory. A wholesaler sells electrical materials to a hardware retailer. A packaging company supplies cartons to a food manufacturer. A commercial cleaning company provides services to an office. A machinery supplier sells equipment to a manufacturing unit. In each example, the transaction takes place between businesses rather than between a business and an individual consumer. B2B transactions can involve one-time purchases, regular supply agreements, bulk orders, service contracts or long-term business relationships. How Does a B2B Business Model Work? A typical B2B transaction involves several steps. The exact process depends on the product, service and agreement between the businesses. 1. A Business Identifies a Requirement A buyer identifies a product or service needed for its operations. For example, a manufacturing company may need industrial motors, safety equipment or packaging materials. 2. The Buyer Searches for Suppliers The buyer identifies potential manufacturers, distributors, wholesalers or service providers. It may use business directories, industry networks, referrals, trade exhibitions or online B2B platforms. 3. The Buyer Requests Quotations The buyer shares its requirements with selected suppliers. The enquiry may include product specifications, quantity, delivery location, expected delivery date and other requirements. 4. Suppliers Provide Quotations Suppliers respond with pricing and relevant commercial details. A quotation may include product cost, taxes, transportation, delivery time, payment terms and warranty conditions. 5. The Buyer Evaluates the Offers The buyer compares quotations and checks whether suppliers can meet the required specifications. Price is important, but it should not be the only selection factor. 6. Both Businesses Agree on the Order After discussions, the buyer and supplier may confirm the order through a purchase order or another written agreement. They then follow the agreed payment, delivery and service terms. Practical Example: Buying Industrial Pumps Through B2B Consider a hypothetical manufacturing company that needs ten industrial pumps. The company contacts two suppliers and requests quotations for the same technical requirements. The suppliers provide the following illustrative offers: Cost details Supplier A Supplier B Quantity 10 10 Price per pump ₹10,000 ₹9,500 Product value ₹1,00,000 ₹95,000 Illustrative GST at 18% ₹18,000 ₹17,100 Transportation ₹2,000 ₹4,000 Illustrative total ₹1,20,000 ₹1,16,100 Supplier B offers the lower illustrative total. However, the buyer should also compare specifications, product quality, delivery commitments, warranty and supplier credentials. The GST rate of 18% is used only for this example. Actual GST depends on the applicable product or service classification and tax rules. This example shows why B2B buyers should compare the complete quotation rather than choosing a supplier based only on the unit price. What Is B2C? B2C stands for Business-to-Consumer . It describes a business selling products or services directly to individual consumers. Examples include: A clothing store selling a shirt to a customer. A supermarket selling groceries to households. A restaurant serving meals to customers. An online store selling a mobile phone to an individual. A salon providing services to a customer. B2C businesses usually focus on individual customer needs, retail pricing, convenience, customer experience and repeat purchases. Unlike many B2B transactions, B2C purchases often involve smaller quantities and shorter buying decisions. What Is D2C? D2C stands for Direct-to-Consumer . It describes a business selling directly to consumers without relying on traditional intermediaries such as retailers or distributors for that sale. For example, a manufacturer may operate its own website and sell products directly to customers. A D2C business may manage its own: Product branding. Online store. Marketing campaigns. Customer communication. Order processing. Delivery arrangements. After-sales support. D2C can give a brand more direct interaction with customers. However, the business must also manage the costs and responsibilities involved in reaching and serving those customers. A business can use more than one model at the same time. For example, a manufacturer may supply bulk orders to distributors through B2B while selling selected products directly to consumers through D2C. Other Business Models You Should Know B2B, B2C and D2C are not the only business models. Other terms also describe how buyers and sellers interact. C2C – Consumer-to-Consumer C2C describes transactions between individual consumers. For example, one person may sell a used bicycle to another person through an online marketplace. C2B – Consumer-to-Business C2B describes individuals providing products or services to businesses. For example, a freelance designer may create a company brochure for a business. B2G – Business-to-Government B2G describes businesses supplying products or services to government departments and public-sector organisations. For example, an equipment manufacturer may supply machinery through a government procurement process. B2B2C – Business-to-Business-to-Consumer B2B2C describes a model in which one business works with another business to reach the final consumer. For example, a food brand may work with a delivery platform to reach customers. How Does B2B Help Businesses Grow? B2B creates opportunities for businesses to connect with other organisations that need their products and services. Its benefits depend on the quality of the product, supplier capabilities, market demand and business relationships. 1. Access to Business Customers Manufacturers, wholesalers and service providers can reach companies that need their products or services. This can help suppliers explore customer segments beyond individual retail buyers. 2. Opportunities for Bulk Orders Many commercial buyers purchase materials and equipment in larger quantities. Suppliers that can meet these requirements may develop regular business relationships. However, order quantities and purchase frequency vary by industry. 3. Repeat Business Opportunities Businesses often need recurring supplies. For example, factories may regularly purchase packaging materials, maintenance supplies and replacement components. Reliable service and consistent product quality can help suppliers build long-term relationships. 4. Better Business Networking B2B activities allow businesses to connect with manufacturers, distributors, wholesalers, contractors and service providers. These connections may create opportunities for supply partnerships and future enquiries. 5. Wider Market Discovery Online business directories and marketplaces can help suppliers present their offerings to buyers who are searching for specific products or services. The actual results depend on visibility, buyer demand, listing quality and the supplier’s response. How Does B2B Help Buyers? B2B is not only useful for suppliers. It also helps buyers identify potential sources for their business requirements. 1. Discover Multiple Suppliers Buyers can explore different manufacturers, wholesalers and service providers before making a decision. 2. Compare Quotations Buyers can request quotations from multiple suppliers and compare pricing, specifications and delivery terms. 3. Find Specialised Products Some industrial and commercial requirements need specific products or technical capabilities. A focused supplier search can help buyers identify businesses that offer relevant products. 4. Understand Market Options By reviewing different suppliers, buyers can learn about available product variations, specifications and commercial terms. 5. Build Supplier Relationships A suitable supplier may become a regular source for materials, equipment or services. Buyers should assess supplier suitability carefully before entering a long-term arrangement. How to Find the Right B2B Supplier Choosing a supplier requires more than comparing prices. Buyers should review the supplier’s ability to meet their actual requirements. Use this checklist before placing an order. 1. Confirm the Product or Service Specifications Clearly identify the required dimensions, material, grade, capacity, model, quantity or service scope. Share drawings or technical documents when necessary. 2. Check Business Details Review the supplier’s business name, address, contact details and available registration information. Where applicable, independently verify GST details and other relevant documents. 3. Request a Detailed Quotation Ask the supplier to mention: Product or service description. Quantity and unit price. Applicable taxes. Transportation and delivery charges. Delivery schedule. Payment terms. Warranty or service conditions. 4. Compare More Than One Supplier Request quotations from multiple suitable suppliers. Compare the complete cost and commercial terms rather than selecting the lowest price automatically. 5. Ask for Product Samples or Demonstrations For important purchases, request samples, product demonstrations or technical documents when practical. This can help assess whether the product meets your requirements. 6. Review Previous Work or References For specialised products and services, ask for relevant project details, customer references or examples of previous work. Check the information independently where possible. 7. Confirm the Agreement in Writing Before making payment, document the final product specifications, quantity, price, taxes, delivery schedule and other agreed conditions. For large transactions, consider appropriate contractual and professional advice. How Can Suppliers Improve Their B2B Business Profile? A clear and informative business profile helps potential buyers understand what a supplier offers. Manufacturers, wholesalers, traders and service providers can improve their profiles by providing accurate information. Include a Clear Business Description Explain what the business manufactures, supplies or provides. Avoid vague statements such as “best quality products at the lowest price.” Instead, mention the actual product range, services and industries served. Add Accurate Product Information Each product listing should include relevant details such as: Product name and model. Specifications and dimensions. Material or grade. Available sizes and variations. Minimum order quantity, where applicable. Product images. Relevant technical documents. Provide Genuine Business Photographs Use clear photographs of actual products, manufacturing facilities, completed projects or service work. Do not use unrelated photographs that could mislead buyers. Keep Contact Information Updated Check that business contact details, address and enquiry channels remain accurate. Respond to enquiries with relevant information and realistic timelines. Explain Service Coverage Service providers should mention the locations they actually serve. Manufacturers and suppliers should describe their genuine delivery or distribution coverage. Do not list locations where the business cannot reasonably provide the stated service. What Is a B2B Marketplace? A B2B marketplace is an online platform that helps businesses discover other businesses, products and services. Depending on the platform, features may include: Manufacturer and supplier listings. Product and service catalogues. Business profiles. Search and category browsing. Buyer enquiries. Supplier contact options. Quotation requests. Some B2B marketplaces facilitate transactions directly. Others primarily support business discovery and lead generation. Buyers should understand the platform’s role before using it. A listing or enquiry platform does not automatically guarantee product quality, supplier reliability, delivery or successful transactions. The platform provides business and product or service listings across different categories. Buyers can explore relevant listings and contact businesses through the available enquiry options. Suppliers can create business profiles and present their products or services to potential buyers. TradersInd aims to make business discovery easier by organising supplier information into relevant categories and listings. For Buyers Buyers can use TradersInd to: Explore businesses across product and service categories. Discover potential manufacturers and suppliers. Review available listing information. Send enquiries to relevant businesses. Contact suppliers to discuss requirements. For Suppliers Suppliers can use TradersInd to: Create a business presence online. List relevant products and services. Present business information to potential buyers. Receive enquiries through available platform features. Improve the visibility of their listed offerings. TradersInd operates as a listing and lead-generation platform. Buyers and suppliers communicate directly to discuss specifications, pricing, payment, delivery and other transaction terms. Users should independently verify business details, product claims, credentials and commercial terms before making decisions. A listing or enquiry does not represent a guarantee or endorsement of a supplier. Common B2B Terms Every Buyer and Supplier Should Understand Understanding common commercial terms can make business communication clearer. Term Meaning MOQ Minimum Order Quantity. The smallest quantity a supplier is willing to accept for an order. RFQ Request for Quotation. A buyer’s request for pricing and commercial details. PO Purchase Order. A document issued by a buyer to confirm an order. SKU Stock Keeping Unit. An identification code used to manage a product or variation. Lead Time The expected time between order confirmation and delivery or completion. Credit Terms Agreed payment conditions that allow payment after a specified period, subject to the agreement. OEM Original Equipment Manufacturer. A company that manufactures products or components for use under its own or another company’s brand, depending on the arrangement. GST Invoice A tax invoice issued in accordance with applicable GST requirements. These terms may have different contractual or operational implications depending on the industry and transaction. Common Mistakes in B2B Transactions Both buyers and suppliers can avoid unnecessary problems by communicating clearly. Mistake 1: Choosing Only by the Lowest Price A low quotation may exclude transportation, taxes, installation or other charges. Compare the complete cost and product specifications. Mistake 2: Sharing Incomplete Requirements A quotation may be inaccurate if the buyer does not provide the required specifications, quantity or delivery location. Share complete information before requesting prices. Mistake 3: Not Checking Supplier Details Do not rely only on a website listing or a phone conversation. Verify relevant business information and documents before making significant payments. Mistake 4: Ignoring Delivery Commitments Confirm stock availability, manufacturing time, dispatch schedule and delivery responsibilities. Record important commitments in writing. Mistake 5: Not Documenting the Agreement Verbal discussions can lead to misunderstandings. Keep written records of the final quotation, purchase order, payment terms and agreed specifications. Mistake 6: Delayed Communication Suppliers should respond to enquiries with accurate information. Buyers should also provide clear requirements and reasonable response timelines. Frequently Asked Questions About B2B 1. What Does B2B Stand For? B2B stands for Business-to-Business. It refers to commercial transactions between two businesses, such as a manufacturer supplying products to a factory. 2. What Is the Difference Between B2B and B2C? B2B involves one business selling products or services to another business. B2C involves a business selling directly to individual consumers. 3. What Is the Difference Between B2B and D2C? B2B focuses on transactions between businesses. D2C describes a brand or manufacturer selling directly to consumers without traditional intermediaries for that sale. 4. Is B2B Suitable for Small Businesses? Yes. Small manufacturers, wholesalers, traders, distributors and service providers can participate in B2B markets. The suitable approach depends on their products, capabilities, pricing and target customers. 5. What Products Are Commonly Sold Through B2B? Examples include industrial machinery, electrical equipment, construction materials, packaging products, safety equipment, raw materials, office supplies and commercial cleaning products. The available categories vary across industries and marketplaces. 6. How Do B2B Buyers Find Suppliers? Buyers can use business directories, online marketplaces, industry associations, trade exhibitions, referrals and direct business networks. They should compare suitable suppliers and verify relevant details before ordering. 7. What Is a B2B Marketplace? A B2B marketplace is an online platform that helps businesses discover suppliers, products and services. Some platforms also support transactions, while others focus on listings and enquiries. 8. Does a B2B Listing Guarantee a Supplier’s Quality? No. A listing alone does not guarantee product quality, business credentials, delivery or transaction outcomes. Buyers should conduct their own checks before placing an order. 9. Can Manufacturers and Wholesalers List Their Products Online? Yes. Manufacturers and wholesalers can use suitable business directories and marketplaces to present product information and connect with potential buyers. They should keep listings accurate and up to date. 10. What Should a Buyer Include in a B2B Enquiry? A useful enquiry should include the required product or service, specifications, quantity, delivery location, expected timeline and any relevant technical requirements. Clear enquiries help suppliers provide more relevant responses. Conclusion B2B, B2C and D2C describe different ways businesses reach their customers. B2B connects businesses with other businesses for products, services and commercial requirements. B2C focuses on sales to individual consumers, while D2C allows brands to sell directly to consumers. For buyers, a well-planned B2B process can make supplier discovery and quotation comparison more organised. For suppliers, accurate product information and clear communication can support stronger business relationships. Understanding these models helps businesses make informed decisions about sourcing, selling and building commercial relationships. B2B stands for Business-to-Business . It describes commercial transactions between two businesses. In this model, one business supplies products or services to another business. A Business Identifies a Requirement A buyer identifies a product or service needed for its operations. For example, a manufacturing company may need industrial motors, safety equipment or packaging materials. 2. A Practical Guide to B2B, B2C and D2C Business Models Understand the differences between B2B, B2C and D2C business models. Businesses use different models to sell products and services. Some sell directly to individual customers. Others supply products to retailers, manufacturers, distributors and commercial buyers. Understanding these business models helps business owners choose the right customers, suppliers and sales channels. Three commonly used terms are B2B, B2C and D2C . Although they all describe commercial activities, they work in different ways. This guide explains what B2B means, how it differs from B2C and D2C, how businesses work with suppliers, and what buyers should consider before placing an order. What Is B2B? B2B stands for Business-to-Business . It describes commercial transactions between two businesses. In this model, one business supplies products or services to another business. The buyer may use those products in its operations, manufacture another product, resell them or deliver services to its own customers. For example: A manufacturer supplies industrial pumps to a factory. A wholesaler sells electrical materials to a hardware retailer. A packaging company supplies cartons to a food manufacturer. A commercial cleaning company provides services to an office. A machinery supplier sells equipment to a manufacturing unit. In each example, the transaction takes place between businesses rather than between a business and an individual consumer. B2B transactions can involve one-time purchases, regular supply agreements, bulk orders, service contracts or long-term business relationships. How Does a B2B Business Model Work? A typical B2B transaction involves several steps. The exact process depends on the product, service and agreement between the businesses. 1. A Business Identifies a Requirement A buyer identifies a product or service needed for its operations. For example, a manufacturing company may need industrial motors, safety equipment or packaging materials. 2. The Buyer Searches for Suppliers The buyer identifies potential manufacturers, distributors, wholesalers or service providers. It may use business directories, industry networks, referrals, trade exhibitions or online B2B platforms. 3. The Buyer Requests Quotations The buyer shares its requirements with selected suppliers. The enquiry may include product specifications, quantity, delivery location, expected delivery date and other requirements. 4. Suppliers Provide Quotations Suppliers respond with pricing and relevant commercial details. A quotation may include product cost, taxes, transportation, delivery time, payment terms and warranty conditions. 5. The Buyer Evaluates the Offers The buyer compares quotations and checks whether suppliers can meet the required specifications. Price is important, but it should not be the only selection factor. 6. Both Businesses Agree on the Order After discussions, the buyer and supplier may confirm the order through a purchase order or another written agreement. They then follow the agreed payment, delivery and service terms. Practical Example: Buying Industrial Pumps Through B2B Consider a hypothetical manufacturing company that needs ten industrial pumps. The company contacts two suppliers and requests quotations for the same technical requirements. However, the buyer should also compare specifications, product quality, delivery commitments, warranty and supplier credentials. The GST rate of 18% is used only for this example. Actual GST depends on the applicable product or service classification and tax rules. This example shows why B2B buyers should compare the complete quotation rather than choosing a supplier based only on the unit price. What Is B2C? B2C stands for Business-to-Consumer . It describes a business selling products or services directly to individual consumers. Examples include: A clothing store selling a shirt to a customer. A supermarket selling groceries to households. A restaurant serving meals to customers. An online store selling a mobile phone to an individual. A salon providing services to a customer. B2C businesses usually focus on individual customer needs, retail pricing, convenience, customer experience and repeat purchases. Unlike many B2B transactions, B2C purchases often involve smaller quantities and shorter buying decisions. What Is D2C? D2C stands for Direct-to-Consumer . It describes a business selling directly to consumers without relying on traditional intermediaries such as retailers or distributors for that sale. For example, a manufacturer may operate its own website and sell products directly to customers. A D2C business may manage its own: Product branding. Online store. Marketing campaigns. Customer communication. Order processing. Delivery arrangements. After-sales support. D2C can give a brand more direct interaction with customers. However, the business must also manage the costs and responsibilities involved in reaching and serving those customers. A business can use more than one model at the same time. B2G – Business-to-Government B2G describes businesses supplying products or services to government departments and public-sector organisations. A Practical Guide to B2B, B2C and D2C Business Models By Team TradersInd / November 5, 2026 What Is B2B? A Practical Guide to B2B, B2C and D2C Business Models Understand the differences between B2B, B2C and D2C business models. Businesses use different models to sell products and services. Some sell directly to individual customers. Others supply products to retailers, manufacturers, distributors and commercial buyers. Understanding these business models helps business owners choose the right customers, suppliers and sales channels. Three commonly used terms are B2B, B2C and D2C . Although they all describe commercial activities, they work in different ways. This guide explains what B2B means, how it differs from B2C and D2C, how businesses work with suppliers, and what buyers should consider before placing an order. What Is B2B? B2B stands for Business-to-Business . It describes commercial transactions between two businesses. In this model, one business supplies products or services to another business. The buyer may use those products in its operations, manufacture another product, resell them or deliver services to its own customers. For example: A manufacturer supplies industrial pumps to a factory. A wholesaler sells electrical materials to a hardware retailer. A packaging company supplies cartons to a food manufacturer. A commercial cleaning company provides services to an office. A machinery supplier sells equipment to a manufacturing unit. In each example, the transaction takes place between businesses rather than between a business and an individual consumer. B2B transactions can involve one-time purchases, regular supply agreements, bulk orders, service contracts or long-term business relationships. How Does a B2B Business Model Work? A typical B2B transaction involves several steps. The exact process depends on the product, service and agreement between the businesses. 1. A Business Identifies a Requirement A buyer identifies a product or service needed for its operations. For example, a manufacturing company may need industrial motors, safety equipment or packaging materials. 2. The Buyer Searches for Suppliers The buyer identifies potential manufacturers, distributors, wholesalers or service providers. It may use business directories, industry networks, referrals, trade exhibitions or online B2B platforms. 3. The Buyer Requests Quotations The buyer shares its requirements with selected suppliers. The enquiry may include product specifications, quantity, delivery location, expected delivery date and other requirements. 4. Suppliers Provide Quotations Suppliers respond with pricing and relevant commercial details. A quotation may include product cost, taxes, transportation, delivery time, payment terms and warranty conditions. 5. The Buyer Evaluates the Offers The buyer compares quotations and checks whether suppliers can meet the required specifications. Price is important, but it should not be the only selection factor. 6. Both Businesses Agree on the Order After discussions, the buyer and supplier may confirm the order through a purchase order or another written agreement. They then follow the agreed payment, delivery and service terms. Practical Example: Buying Industrial Pumps Through B2B Consider a hypothetical manufacturing company that needs ten industrial pumps. The company contacts two suppliers and requests quotations for the same technical requirements. The suppliers provide the following illustrative offers: Cost details Supplier A Supplier B Quantity 10 10 Price per pump ₹10,000 ₹9,500 Product value ₹1,00,000 ₹95,000 Illustrative GST at 18% ₹18,000 ₹17,100 Transportation ₹2,000 ₹4,000 Illustrative total ₹1,20,000 ₹1,16,100 Supplier B offers the lower illustrative total. However, the buyer should also compare specifications, product quality, delivery commitments, warranty and supplier credentials. The GST rate of 18% is used only for this example. Actual GST depends on the applicable product or service classification and tax rules. This example shows why B2B buyers should compare the complete quotation rather than choosing a supplier based only on the unit price. What Is B2C? B2C stands for Business-to-Consumer . It describes a business selling products or services directly to individual consumers. Examples include: A clothing store selling a shirt to a customer. A supermarket selling groceries to households. A restaurant serving meals to customers. An online store selling a mobile phone to an individual. A salon providing services to a customer. B2C businesses usually focus on individual customer needs, retail pricing, convenience, customer experience and repeat purchases. Unlike many B2B transactions, B2C purchases often involve smaller quantities and shorter buying decisions. What Is D2C? D2C stands for Direct-to-Consumer . It describes a business selling directly to consumers without relying on traditional intermediaries such as retailers or distributors for that sale. For example, a manufacturer may operate its own website and sell products directly to customers. A D2C business may manage its own: Product branding. Online store. Marketing campaigns. Customer communication. Order processing. Delivery arrangements. After-sales support. D2C can give a brand more direct interaction with customers. However, the business must also manage the costs and responsibilities involved in reaching and serving those customers. A business can use more than one model at the same time. Find Specialised Products Some industrial and commercial requirements need specific products or technical capabilities. Add Accurate Product Information Each product listing should include relevant details such as: Product name and model. Specifications and dimensions. Material or grade. Supplier contact options. Quotation requests. Some B2B marketplaces facilitate transactions directly. Others primarily support business discovery and lead generation. Buyers should understand the platform’s role before using it. A listing or enquiry platform does not automatically guarantee product quality, supplier reliability, delivery or successful transactions. The platform provides business and product or service listings across different categories. Buyers can explore relevant listings and contact businesses through the available enquiry options. Suppliers can create business profiles and present their products or services to potential buyers. TradersInd aims to make business discovery easier by organising supplier information into relevant categories and listings. Send enquiries to relevant businesses. Contact suppliers to discuss requirements. For Suppliers Suppliers can use TradersInd to: Create a business presence online. List relevant products and services. Present business information to potential buyers. Receive enquiries through available platform features. Improve the visibility of their listed offerings. TradersInd operates as a listing and lead-generation platform. Buyers and suppliers communicate directly to discuss specifications, pricing, payment, delivery and other transaction terms. Users should independently verify business details, product claims, credentials and commercial terms before making decisions. A listing or enquiry does not represent a guarantee or endorsement of a supplier. Common B2B Terms Every Buyer and Supplier Should Understand Understanding common commercial terms can make business communication clearer. Term Meaning MOQ Minimum Order Quantity. The smallest quantity a supplier is willing to accept for an order. RFQ Request for Quotation. A buyer’s request for pricing and commercial details. PO Purchase Order. A document issued by a buyer to confirm an order. SKU Stock Keeping Unit. An identification code used to manage a product or variation. Lead Time The expected time between order confirmation and delivery or completion. Credit Terms Agreed payment conditions that allow payment after a specified period, subject to the agreement. OEM Original Equipment Manufacturer. A company that manufactures products or components for use under its own or another company’s brand, depending on the arrangement. GST Invoice A tax invoice issued in accordance with applicable GST requirements. These terms may have different contractual or operational implications depending on the industry and transaction. Common Mistakes in B2B Transactions Both buyers and suppliers can avoid unnecessary problems by communicating clearly. Mistake 1: Choosing Only by the Lowest Price A low quotation may exclude transportation, taxes, installation or other charges. Compare the complete cost and product specifications. Mistake 2: Sharing Incomplete Requirements A quotation may be inaccurate if the buyer does not provide the required specifications, quantity or delivery location. Share complete information before requesting prices. Mistake 3: Not Checking Supplier Details Do not rely only on a website listing or a phone conversation. Verify relevant business information and documents before making significant payments. Mistake 4: Ignoring Delivery Commitments Confirm stock availability, manufacturing time, dispatch schedule and delivery responsibilities. Record important commitments in writing. Mistake 5: Not Documenting the Agreement Verbal discussions can lead to misunderstandings. Keep written records of the final quotation, purchase order, payment terms and agreed specifications. Mistake 6: Delayed Communication Suppliers should respond to enquiries with accurate information. Buyers should also provide clear requirements and reasonable response timelines. It refers to commercial transactions between two businesses, such as a manufacturer supplying products to a factory. 2. What Is the Difference Between B2B and B2C? B2B focuses on transactions between businesses. D2C describes a brand or manufacturer selling directly to consumers without traditional intermediaries for that sale. 4. The suitable approach depends on their products, capabilities, pricing and target customers. 5. What Products Are Commonly Sold Through B2B? Examples include industrial machinery, electrical equipment, construction materials, packaging products, safety equipment, raw materials, office supplies and commercial cleaning products. Buyers should conduct their own checks before placing an order. 9. Can Manufacturers and Wholesalers List Their Products Online? Yes. Manufacturers and wholesalers can use suitable business directories and marketplaces to present product information and connect with potential buyers. They should keep listings accurate and up to date. 10. What Should a Buyer Include in a B2B Enquiry? A useful enquiry should include the required product or service, specifications, quantity, delivery location, expected timeline and any relevant technical requirements. A Practical Guide to B2B, B2C and D2C Business Models Understand the differences between B2B, B2C and D2C business models. Businesses use different models to sell products and services. Some sell directly to individual customers. Others supply products to retailers, manufacturers, distributors and commercial buyers. Understanding these business models helps business owners choose the right customers, suppliers and sales channels. Three commonly used terms are B2B, B2C and D2C . Although they all describe commercial activities, they work in different ways. This guide explains what B2B means, how it differs from B2C and D2C, how businesses work with suppliers, and what buyers should consider before placing an order. What Is B2B? B2B stands for Business-to-Business . It describes commercial transactions between two businesses. In this model, one business supplies products or services to another business. The buyer may use those products in its operations, manufacture another product, resell them or deliver services to its own customers. For example: A manufacturer supplies industrial pumps to a factory. A wholesaler sells electrical materials to a hardware retailer. A packaging company supplies cartons to a food manufacturer. A commercial cleaning company provides services to an office. A machinery supplier sells equipment to a manufacturing unit. In each example, the transaction takes place between businesses rather than between a business and an individual consumer. B2B transactions can involve one-time purchases, regular supply agreements, bulk orders, service contracts or long-term business relationships. How Does a B2B Business Model Work? A typical B2B transaction involves several steps. The exact process depends on the product, service and agreement between the businesses. 1. A Business Identifies a Requirement A buyer identifies a product or service needed for its operations. For example, a manufacturing company may need industrial motors, safety equipment or packaging materials. 2. The Buyer Searches for Suppliers The buyer identifies potential manufacturers, distributors, wholesalers or service providers. It may use business directories, industry networks, referrals, trade exhibitions or online B2B platforms. 3. The Buyer Requests Quotations The buyer shares its requirements with selected suppliers. The enquiry may include product specifications, quantity, delivery location, expected delivery date and other requirements. 4. Suppliers Provide Quotations Suppliers respond with pricing and relevant commercial details. A quotation may include product cost, taxes, transportation, delivery time, payment terms and warranty conditions. 5. The Buyer Evaluates the Offers The buyer compares quotations and checks whether suppliers can meet the required specifications. Price is important, but it should not be the only selection factor. 6. Both Businesses Agree on the Order After discussions, the buyer and supplier may confirm the order through a purchase order or another written agreement. They then follow the agreed payment, delivery and service terms. Practical Example: Buying Industrial Pumps Through B2B Consider a hypothetical manufacturing company that needs ten industrial pumps. The company contacts two suppliers and requests quotations for the same technical requirements. The suppliers provide the following illustrative offers: Cost details Supplier A Supplier B Quantity 10 10 Price per pump ₹10,000 ₹9,500 Product value ₹1,00,000 ₹95,000 Illustrative GST at 18% ₹18,000 ₹17,100 Transportation ₹2,000 ₹4,000 Illustrative total ₹1,20,000 ₹1,16,100 Supplier B offers the lower illustrative total. However, the buyer should also compare specifications, product quality, delivery commitments, warranty and supplier credentials. The GST rate of 18% is used only for this example. Actual GST depends on the applicable product or service classification and tax rules. This example shows why B2B buyers should compare the complete quotation rather than choosing a supplier based only on the unit price. What Is B2C? B2C stands for Business-to-Consumer . It describes a business selling products or services directly to individual consumers. Examples include: A clothing store selling a shirt to a customer. A supermarket selling groceries to households. A restaurant serving meals to customers. An online store selling a mobile phone to an individual. A salon providing services to a customer. B2C businesses usually focus on individual customer needs, retail pricing, convenience, customer experience and repeat purchases. Unlike many B2B transactions, B2C purchases often involve smaller quantities and shorter buying decisions. What Is D2C? D2C stands for Direct-to-Consumer . It describes a business selling directly to consumers without relying on traditional intermediaries such as retailers or distributors for that sale. For example, a manufacturer may operate its own website and sell products directly to customers. A D2C business may manage its own: Product branding. Online store. Marketing campaigns. Customer communication. Order processing. Delivery arrangements. After-sales support. D2C can give a brand more direct interaction with customers. However, the business must also manage the costs and responsibilities involved in reaching and serving those customers. A business can use more than one model at the same time. For example, a manufacturer may supply bulk orders to distributors through B2B while selling selected products directly to consumers through D2C. Other Business Models You Should Know B2B, B2C and D2C are not the only business models. Other terms also describe how buyers and sellers interact. C2C – Consumer-to-Consumer C2C describes transactions between individual consumers. For example, one person may sell a used bicycle to another person through an online marketplace. C2B – Consumer-to-Business C2B describes individuals providing products or services to businesses. For example, a freelance designer may create a company brochure for a business. B2G – Business-to-Government B2G describes businesses supplying products or services to government departments and public-sector organisations. For example, an equipment manufacturer may supply machinery through a government procurement process. B2B2C – Business-to-Business-to-Consumer B2B2C describes a model in which one business works with another business to reach the final consumer. For example, a food brand may work with a delivery platform to reach customers. How Does B2B Help Businesses Grow? B2B creates opportunities for businesses to connect with other organisations that need their products and services. Its benefits depend on the quality of the product, supplier capabilities, market demand and business relationships. 1. Access to Business Customers Manufacturers, wholesalers and service providers can reach companies that need their products or services. This can help suppliers explore customer segments beyond individual retail buyers. 2. Opportunities for Bulk Orders Many commercial buyers purchase materials and equipment in larger quantities. Suppliers that can meet these requirements may develop regular business relationships. However, order quantities and purchase frequency vary by industry. 3. Repeat Business Opportunities Businesses often need recurring supplies. For example, factories may regularly purchase packaging materials, maintenance supplies and replacement components. Reliable service and consistent product quality can help suppliers build long-term relationships. 4. Better Business Networking B2B activities allow businesses to connect with manufacturers, distributors, wholesalers, contractors and service providers. These connections may create opportunities for supply partnerships and future enquiries. 5. Wider Market Discovery Online business directories and marketplaces can help suppliers present their offerings to buyers who are searching for specific products or services. The actual results depend on visibility, buyer demand, listing quality and the supplier’s response. How Does B2B Help Buyers? B2B is not only useful for suppliers. It also helps buyers identify potential sources for their business requirements. 1. Discover Multiple Suppliers Buyers can explore different manufacturers, wholesalers and service providers before making a decision. 2. Compare Quotations Buyers can request quotations from multiple suppliers and compare pricing, specifications and delivery terms. 3. Find Specialised Products Some industrial and commercial requirements need specific products or technical capabilities. A focused supplier search can help buyers identify businesses that offer relevant products. 4. Understand Market Options By reviewing different suppliers, buyers can learn about available product variations, specifications and commercial terms. 5. Build Supplier Relationships A suitable supplier may become a regular source for materials, equipment or services. Buyers should assess supplier suitability carefully before entering a long-term arrangement. How to Find the Right B2B Supplier Choosing a supplier requires more than comparing prices. Buyers should review the supplier’s ability to meet their actual requirements. Use this checklist before placing an order. 1. Confirm the Product or Service Specifications Clearly identify the required dimensions, material, grade, capacity, model, quantity or service scope. Share drawings or technical documents when necessary. 2. Check Business Details Review the supplier’s business name, address, contact details and available registration information. Where applicable, independently verify GST details and other relevant documents. 3. Request a Detailed Quotation Ask the supplier to mention: Product or service description. Quantity and unit price. Applicable taxes. Transportation and delivery charges. Delivery schedule. Payment terms. Warranty or service conditions. 4. Compare More Than One Supplier Request quotations from multiple suitable suppliers. Compare the complete cost and commercial terms rather than selecting the lowest price automatically. 5. Ask for Product Samples or Demonstrations For important purchases, request samples, product demonstrations or technical documents when practical. This can help assess whether the product meets your requirements. 6. Review Previous Work or References For specialised products and services, ask for relevant project details, customer references or examples of previous work. Check the information independently where possible. 7. Confirm the Agreement in Writing Before making payment, document the final product specifications, quantity, price, taxes, delivery schedule and other agreed conditions. For large transactions, consider appropriate contractual and professional advice. How Can Suppliers Improve Their B2B Business Profile? A clear and informative business profile helps potential buyers understand what a supplier offers. Manufacturers, wholesalers, traders and service providers can improve their profiles by providing accurate information. Include a Clear Business Description Explain what the business manufactures, supplies or provides. Avoid vague statements such as “best quality products at the lowest price.” Instead, mention the actual product range, services and industries served. Add Accurate Product Information Each product listing should include relevant details such as: Product name and model. Specifications and dimensions. Material or grade. Available sizes and variations. Minimum order quantity, where applicable. Product images. Relevant technical documents. Provide Genuine Business Photographs Use clear photographs of actual products, manufacturing facilities, completed projects or service work. Do not use unrelated photographs that could mislead buyers. Keep Contact Information Updated Check that business contact details, address and enquiry channels remain accurate. Respond to enquiries with relevant information and realistic timelines. Explain Service Coverage Service providers should mention the locations they actually serve. Manufacturers and suppliers should describe their genuine delivery or distribution coverage. Do not list locations where the business cannot reasonably provide the stated service. Depending on the platform, features may include: Manufacturer and supplier listings. Product and service catalogues. Business profiles. Search and category browsing. Buyer enquiries. Supplier contact options. Quotation requests. Some B2B marketplaces facilitate transactions directly. Others primarily support business discovery and lead generation. Buyers should understand the platform’s role before using it. A listing or enquiry platform does not automatically guarantee product quality, supplier reliability, delivery or successful transactions. The platform provides business and product or service listings across different categories. Buyers can explore relevant listings and contact businesses through the available enquiry options. Suppliers can create business profiles and present their products or services to potential buyers. TradersInd aims to make business discovery easier by organising supplier information into relevant categories and listings. For Buyers Buyers can use TradersInd to: Explore businesses across product and service categories. Discover potential manufacturers and suppliers. Review available listing information. Send enquiries to relevant businesses. Contact suppliers to discuss requirements. For Suppliers Suppliers can use TradersInd to: Create a business presence online. List relevant products and services. Present business information to potential buyers. Receive enquiries through available platform features. Improve the visibility of their listed offerings. TradersInd operates as a listing and lead-generation platform. Buyers and suppliers communicate directly to discuss specifications, pricing, payment, delivery and other transaction terms. Users should independently verify business details, product claims, credentials and commercial terms before making decisions. A listing or enquiry does not represent a guarantee or endorsement of a supplier. Common B2B Terms Every Buyer and Supplier Should Understand Understanding common commercial terms can make business communication clearer. Term Meaning MOQ Minimum Order Quantity. The smallest quantity a supplier is willing to accept for an order. RFQ Request for Quotation. A buyer’s request for pricing and commercial details. PO Purchase Order. A document issued by a buyer to confirm an order. SKU Stock Keeping Unit. An identification code used to manage a product or variation. Lead Time The expected time between order confirmation and delivery or completion. Credit Terms Agreed payment conditions that allow payment after a specified period, subject to the agreement. OEM Original Equipment Manufacturer. A company that manufactures products or components for use under its own or another company’s brand, depending on the arrangement. GST Invoice A tax invoice issued in accordance with applicable GST requirements. These terms may have different contractual or operational implications depending on the industry and transaction. Common Mistakes in B2B Transactions Both buyers and suppliers can avoid unnecessary problems by communicating clearly. Mistake 1: Choosing Only by the Lowest Price A low quotation may exclude transportation, taxes, installation or other charges. Compare the complete cost and product specifications. Mistake 2: Sharing Incomplete Requirements A quotation may be inaccurate if the buyer does not provide the required specifications, quantity or delivery location. Share complete information before requesting prices. Mistake 3: Not Checking Supplier Details Do not rely only on a website listing or a phone conversation. Verify relevant business information and documents before making significant payments. Mistake 4: Ignoring Delivery Commitments Confirm stock availability, manufacturing time, dispatch schedule and delivery responsibilities. Record important commitments in writing. Mistake 5: Not Documenting the Agreement Verbal discussions can lead to misunderstandings. Keep written records of the final quotation, purchase order, payment terms and agreed specifications. Mistake 6: Delayed Communication Suppliers should respond to enquiries with accurate information. Buyers should also provide clear requirements and reasonable response timelines. Frequently Asked Questions About B2B 1. What Does B2B Stand For? B2B stands for Business-to-Business. It refers to commercial transactions between two businesses, such as a manufacturer supplying products to a factory. 2. What Is the Difference Between B2B and B2C? B2B involves one business selling products or services to another business. B2C involves a business selling directly to individual consumers. 3. What Is the Difference Between B2B and D2C? B2B focuses on transactions between businesses. D2C describes a brand or manufacturer selling directly to consumers without traditional intermediaries for that sale. 4. Is B2B Suitable for Small Businesses? Yes. Small manufacturers, wholesalers, traders, distributors and service providers can participate in B2B markets. The suitable approach depends on their products, capabilities, pricing and target customers. 5. What Products Are Commonly Sold Through B2B? Examples include industrial machinery, electrical equipment, construction materials, packaging products, safety equipment, raw materials, office supplies and commercial cleaning products. The available categories vary across industries and marketplaces. 6. How Do B2B Buyers Find Suppliers? Buyers can use business directories, online marketplaces, industry associations, trade exhibitions, referrals and direct business networks. They should compare suitable suppliers and verify relevant details before ordering. 7. What Is a B2B Marketplace? A B2B marketplace is an online platform that helps businesses discover suppliers, products and services. Some platforms also support transactions, while others focus on listings and enquiries. 8. Does a B2B Listing Guarantee a Supplier’s Quality? No. A listing alone does not guarantee product quality, business credentials, delivery or transaction outcomes. Buyers should conduct their own checks before placing an order. 9. Can Manufacturers and Wholesalers List Their Products Online? Yes. Manufacturers and wholesalers can use suitable business directories and marketplaces to present product information and connect with potential buyers. They should keep listings accurate and up to date. 10. What Should a Buyer Include in a B2B Enquiry? A useful enquiry should include the required product or service, specifications, quantity, delivery location, expected timeline and any relevant technical requirements. Clear enquiries help suppliers provide more relevant responses. Conclusion B2B, B2C and D2C describe different ways businesses reach their customers. B2B connects businesses with other businesses for products, services and commercial requirements. B2C focuses on sales to individual consumers, while D2C allows brands to sell directly to consumers. For buyers, a well-planned B2B process can make supplier discovery and quotation comparison more organised. For suppliers, accurate product information and clear communication can support stronger business relationships. Understanding these models helps businesses make informed decisions about sourcing, selling and building commercial relationships. B2B stands for Business-to-Business . It describes commercial transactions between two businesses. In this model, one business supplies products or services to another business. The buyer may use those products in its operations, manufacture another product, resell them or deliver services to its own customers. For example: A manufacturer supplies industrial pumps to a factory. A wholesaler sells electrical materials to a hardware retailer. A packaging company supplies cartons to a food manufacturer. A commercial cleaning company provides services to an office. A machinery supplier sells equipment to a manufacturing unit. In each example, the transaction takes place between businesses rather than between a business and an individual consumer. B2B transactions can involve one-time purchases, regular supply agreements, bulk orders, service contracts or long-term business relationships. How Does a B2B Business Model Work? A typical B2B transaction involves several steps. The exact process depends on the product, service and agreement between the businesses. 1. A Business Identifies a Requirement A buyer identifies a product or service needed for its operations. For example, a manufacturing company may need industrial motors, safety equipment or packaging materials. 2. The Buyer Searches for Suppliers The buyer identifies potential manufacturers, distributors, wholesalers or service providers. It may use business directories, industry networks, referrals, trade exhibitions or online B2B platforms. 3. The Buyer Requests Quotations The buyer shares its requirements with selected suppliers. The enquiry may include product specifications, quantity, delivery location, expected delivery date and other requirements. 4. Suppliers Provide Quotations Suppliers respond with pricing and relevant commercial details. A quotation may include product cost, taxes, transportation, delivery time, payment terms and warranty conditions. 5. A restaurant serving meals to customers. An online store selling a mobile phone to an individual. A salon providing services to a customer. B2C businesses usually focus on individual customer needs, retail pricing, convenience, customer experience and repeat purchases. It describes a business selling directly to consumers without relying on traditional intermediaries such as retailers or distributors for that sale. For example, a manufacturer may operate its own website and sell products directly to customers. A D2C business may manage its own: Product branding. Online store. Marketing campaigns. Customer communication. Order processing. Delivery arrangements. After-sales support. D2C can give a brand more direct interaction with customers.
